title: Lean BA Planning: Who to Learn From, and How
summary: Lean BA planning in practice: decide what you need to learn, map stakeholders beyond names, pick predictive or adaptive rhythm and match elicitation to the question.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say you're the BA on a new claims project, and it's Monday. Your calendar has three interviews, one workshop, a backlog refinement and a review with operations. By Wednesday you've heard the same problem described five ways. Operations says claims take too long. Agents say the screens are a maze. Compliance says nobody can prove who approved what. Finance mentions "leakage" and doesn't explain. Engineering says the core system can't be touched before Q3.

None of them is wrong. Each one is describing the part of the problem they live with every day. The job this week is to figure out who you need to learn from, in what order, and how. That's what BA planning is for, and it's the second post in the Lean BA series, after starting from value.

About the sources: This series grew out of my notes on Lean Business Analysis, which pull from Emrah Yayici's BA material, PMI and Business Analysis For Dummies (Kupersmith, Mulvey and McGoey). For this post I checked the planning and elicitation ideas against the IIBA's BABOK Guide v3 and the For Dummies authors' own articles, linked below.

A BA plan is a plan for learning

A delivery plan says "build the onboarding flow in Sprint 3." A BA plan asks different questions. Who understands onboarding today? Which assumptions are still shaky? Which decisions hang on those assumptions? When do we need to know enough to move?

BABOK v3 opens with exactly this. Its first knowledge area, Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, has you plan the approach, plan how you'll work with stakeholders, plan who decides what, and plan where the information will live, before the analysis itself starts. For a five-person product team that can be one page. For a regulated project with three vendors it needs more. Match the plan to the risk, then stop.

Here's a one-page version that covers most teams:

QuestionWhat goes in the plan
What do we need to learn?How the process runs today, where it hurts, the decision rules, who owns which data, constraints like performance and audit
Who can teach us?Users, their managers, operations, support, compliance, engineering, the teams downstream
How will we learn it?Watching the work, interviews, workshops, reading documents, reviewing a prototype
When do we know enough?When the big risks have names, the options can be compared and the next slice of delivery is clear

Stakeholders are more than names on a list

A stakeholder list with names and emails is a phone book. What helps is knowing, for each person or group, what they care about, how much say they have, how they feel about the change, when they're available and what kind of evidence convinces them. BABOK's Plan Stakeholder Engagement task asks for the same things: roles, attitudes, decision authority, and level of influence.

Back to the claims project. The head of operations cares about throughput. Frontline agents want fewer screens and less rework. Compliance wants an audit trail. Finance wants to stop money leaking out through wrong payouts. Engineering cares about integration limits. Lump all of them into "business users" and your requirements will look neat on paper, then fall apart the first time two of those interests collide.

A RACI matrix helps here, as long as it doesn't become wall art. BABOK lists it among the stakeholder techniques: who is Responsible for doing the work, who is Accountable and signs off, who must be Consulted, who just needs to be Informed. The table itself is the least interesting part. The value is the slightly awkward conversation it forces early: "Wait, does finance approve this rule, or just get told about it?" Better to have that chat in week one than in UAT.

Predictive and adaptive work need different rhythms

Lean BA doesn't mean every project has to be Agile. BABOK frames the approach as a range. Predictive approaches try to settle uncertainty up front, which pays off when change is expensive, the domain is regulated or many outside parties have to line up. Adaptive approaches deliver in short cycles and work out the details as they go, which pays off when the solution is uncertain and real feedback beats early completeness. Plenty of work sits in between.

ContextBA rhythmTypical artifacts
Predictive projectMore elicitation up front, then a signed-off baselineBRD, requirements package, traceability matrix
Adaptive product workFill in detail just before each sliceUser stories, examples, prototypes, acceptance criteria
Hybrid programBusiness outcomes fixed early, solution detail worked out as you goRoadmap, capability map, a backlog that keeps changing

The trap is pretending one rhythm fits everything. A team building a regulatory report for a bank needs tighter traceability and sign-off than a team testing a new onboarding flow. Both still need the same habits: learn enough, decide honestly, and keep what you've learned where everyone can see it.

Elicitation is more than taking orders

"Gathering requirements" makes it sound like the requirements already exist somewhere, like apples on a tree, and the BA just needs a basket. Elicitation starts from a different assumption: what you need to know is spread across many people, it's partial, sometimes contradictory, and a good chunk of it is habit nobody thinks to mention. BABOK's elicitation area reflects that with three separate steps: prepare, conduct, then confirm what you heard.

So good elicitation starts before the meeting. Decide what you want to come out of it, who needs to be there, what to read first and what you'll produce afterwards. A workshop with no decision to make produces noise. An interview with no context turns into a complaint session. A survey sent too early turns shallow guesses into numbers that look official.

The questions matter too. Open questions bring out context: "Walk me through the last time this went wrong." Closed questions check a fact: "Does every refund over $500 need a manager's approval?" Context-free questions, an idea from Gause and Weinberg's Exploring Requirements, are questions you could ask on any project, and they keep you from jumping to a solution: "What would it look like once this problem is solved?" And "why" questions find causes, but ask them carelessly and people start defending themselves. "What led to that?" usually lands better than "Why did you do that?"

Pick the technique by what you need to learn

There's no single best technique. The Business Analysis For Dummies authors suggest a practical first filter: how many people you need to hear from. Working mostly alone, use document and interface analysis. One or two people, use observation, interviews or a prototype. Five to seven, a workshop or focus group. Ten or more, a survey or a larger workshop (How to Choose an Approach for a Business Analysis). Then adjust for what you're unsure about:

  • Document analysis when policies, contracts, reports or procedures already shape the work.
  • Observation when people can't easily explain what they do, because they do it on autopilot.
  • Interviews when you need depth, nuance or something sensitive.
  • Workshops when a decision crosses roles and the disagreement needs to come out in one room.
  • Surveys when you need breadth and already know what to ask.
  • Prototypes when people need to see something before they can tell you what's missing.
  • Interface analysis when data crosses system boundaries and assumptions hide in the handoffs.

Observation deserves a special mention. The same authors describe three levels: watch without interrupting, watch and ask questions as you go, or do the task yourself. They also flag the catch. People who know they're being watched tend to follow the official process more carefully than usual, and a slow afternoon can look nothing like peak hours (How to Use Observation Methods in Business Analysis).

Here's where it pays off. A warehouse team asks for "fewer clicks." Spend a shift on the floor and you might find the clicks are fine. The real cost is walking distance, a scanner that lags and the exceptions nobody has a screen for. A prototype review alone would have missed all of that. On the other hand, if compliance asks for a "full audit trail," reading the regulation and running a rules workshop will teach you more than any number of user interviews.

A small weekly rhythm

Most teams don't need a heavy process. Something like this is enough:

  1. Map the stakeholders and write down which decisions each one owns.
  2. Run the smallest piece of elicitation that reduces the next risk.
  3. Turn what you learned into a model, an example or a story within a day or two, while it's fresh.
  4. Review it with the people who will use, approve, build, test and run the change.
  5. Keep open assumptions on a visible list until they're proven or someone accepts them on purpose.

This week, take one feature you're working on and fill in the four-row table above for it. If the "Who can teach us?" row has only one name, that's your next meeting. The next post in the series picks up from there: turning what you heard into shared models.

faqs.a: A BA plan describes how the team will learn what it needs before and during delivery: what to find out, from whom, with which techniques, and when it knows enough to move. In BABOK v3 this sits in Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, which covers the approach, stakeholder engagement, governance and where the information lives.

faqs.q: What is stakeholder analysis in business analysis?
faqs.a: It means understanding each person or group affected by a change: what they care about, their attitude to the change, their decision authority and their level of influence. A RACI matrix is one common tool for making decision rights explicit early.

faqs.q: What is the difference between eliciting and gathering requirements?
faqs.a: Gathering suggests requirements already exist and only need collecting. Elicitation assumes what you need to know is spread across people, partial, sometimes contradictory and often unspoken. BABOK splits it into preparing, conducting and confirming elicitation.

faqs.q: How do I choose an elicitation technique?
faqs.a: Start with how many people you need to hear from and what you're unsure about. The Business Analysis For Dummies authors suggest document and interface analysis when working mostly alone, observation, interviews or prototypes for one or two people, workshops or focus groups for five to seven, and surveys or larger workshops for ten or more.
